html:
Muhammad al-Bukhari was a Muslim scholar born in Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan, in 810. He compiled the Sahih al-Bukhari, a collection of the sayings and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad, the hadith. Sunni Muslims hold it to be the most trusted book after the Quran.

Hadith were passed on by word of mouth through chains of named teachers, and by the 9th century many false ones were in circulation. Al-Bukhari spent about sixteen years travelling to collect them: to Mecca and Medina, to Baghdad, Egypt and Syria. Tradition says he gathered hundreds of thousands of reports and checked each chain of teachers with great care, keeping only those he judged sound. His book holds a few thousand.

It became the first of the six canonical hadith books of Sunni Islam, with that of his student Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj close behind.

At the end of his life he fell out with the governor of Bukhara and left. He died in 870 in a village near Samarkand, where his tomb is now a large pilgrimage centre. His life fell in the high age of the Abbasid Caliphate.
